text:
The text presents a contrast between two distinct perspectives on human nature, framed within a disjointed narrative structure. The primary thematic opposition lies between William Golding’s view in 'Lord of the Flies' and Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy. Golding is cited as portraying the theme of inherent evil, suggesting that humans naturally descend into savagery when removed from societal constraints. In direct contrast, Rousseau is presented as arguing that society is the corrupting force, implying that humanity’s natural state is one of goodness and freedom.

In terms of presentation, the text exhibits a significant structural inconsistency. It begins with an unrelated, factual question ("Name the organ that pumps blood") which has no thematic or logical connection to the subsequent literary and philosophical analysis. This abrupt shift creates a jarring transition before the text settles into a comparative analysis of Golding and Rousseau. While the comparison between Golding and Rousseau is clearly articulated using the transitional phrase "Contrarily," the inclusion of the initial medical question undermines the coherence of the overall passage, serving as a distraction rather than a contributing element to the thematic discussion.
